reason: Dropping post-randomization non-adherers breaks the randomized comparison, so a PP estimate alone cannot be checked for selection bias; ITT (analysis by original assignment) is the randomization-respecting anchor and is reported with PP in confirmatory/non-inferiority trials (ICH E9; CONSORT non-inferiority extension). The stated basis is loose, though: CONSORT item 16 asks for denominators and whether analysis was by original groups, and does not itself say PP must accompany ITT; the rule rests on the broader PP-vs-ITT logic, not that item.

citations.cite: Moher et al. 2010 BMJ 340:c869 (CONSORT 2010 E&E), item 16 - article exists, item text not retrieved (403)
ICH E9 (1998) s5.2.1 (FAS and PPS both analysed in confirmatory trials)
Hernan & Robins 2017 NEJM 377:1391 (per-protocol analyses of pragmatic trials)

bite_note: Refuses a PP-only trial sentence; a researcher could otherwise report the (usually more favourable) PP effect alone.

narrowest_regime: QRILC run once, outside the MI loop, with intervals computed from the completed data as if observed
reason: A single stochastic completion treated as observed data ignores between-imputation variance and parameter uncertainty in the fitted truncated-normal, so intervals are too narrow in proportion to the censored fraction; that is Rubin's standard argument against single imputation. (Repeating QRILC m times and pooling would be an improper but better approximation, which is a different pipeline from the one described.)

citations.cite: Rubin 1987 / Little & Rubin, multiple imputation variance decomposition (standard result)

bite_note: Blocks a fill that would give anti-conservative intervals when a sizeable share of a factor is below detection; at very small censored fractions the loss is small.

failing_part: gives near-nominal type I error even with about 12 units, so no small-sample correction of the sandwich is needed
narrowest_regime: Roughly 40+ clusters (Cameron & Miller's rule of thumb is that CR0 with normal reference is only reliable with many clusters); with ~12 units a bias-corrected sandwich (CR2/CR3/Mancl-DeRouen) and a t reference are needed
reason: The sandwich is consistent only as the number of units grows; CR0 is downward biased and the normal reference ignores the variance estimate's own uncertainty. My simulation (12 clusters, exchangeable GEE with robust CR0, nominal 5%) gave 8.8-16.8% rejection across Gaussian/binary, cluster-level/within-cluster covariates, balanced/unbalanced sizes; even a t(G-1) reference left 5.8-12.8%.

citations.cite: Liang & Zeger 1986 Biometrika 73:13 (asymptotic in number of clusters)
Cameron & Miller 2015 J Human Resources 50:317 (few-cluster bias, CR1/CR2/CR3, t reference)
Own simulation gee_sim.py: type I 0.088-0.168 normal-CR0 at G=12

bite_note: Sets the default interval method for clustered data with few units; a CR0/normal default produces intervals that undercover (about 85-91% instead of 95%) and false positives at 2-3x nominal.

failing_part: "and otherwise the MEC examination weight" (interview-only variables take the interview weight); and the least-common-denominator rule is exact only for nested subsamples
narrowest_regime: Variables from exam/lab components, where the nested chain OGTT within fasting within MEC holds, or diet-only analyses (day-1 or two-day dietary weight); interview-only tables use WTINT*
reason: The core rule is CDC's: use the weight of the smallest subsample containing all analysis variables, and WTSAF* (fasting), WTDRD1*/WTDR2D* (dietary) and WTSOG* (OGTT, e.g. OGTT_H 2013-14) are real names (I fetched GLU_J, P_GLU, OGTT_H; no OGTT file exists for 2017-Mar 2020). But CDC points interview-only analyses to the interview weight, not MEC, and fasting plus dietary variables are not nested, so no single named weight is valid there. The 1%/5%/10-row subsample detector is an engineering heuristic (self-described as own tolerance) with no methods justification.

citations.cite: CDC NHANES Tutorials, Weighting Module - 'weight of the smallest subpopulation' (fetched; OGTT weight not mentioned there)
CDC OGTT_H.htm: WTSOG2YR exists; GLU_J.htm / P_GLU.htm: WTSAF2YR / WTSAFPRP
CDC guidance that interview-only analyses use WTINT (not re-fetched; page returned not found)

bite_note: Decides which weight is offered first; MEC for interview-only data loses examined-nonresponders and a fasting+diet merge is silently given one weight that fits neither sample.

reason: A ratio over a zero denominator is undefined, not a measurement, and +/-inf breaks means, scaling and most estimators, so converting it to missing is the correct first repair. The residual caveat is that this missingness is structural (for example a zero-intake day), so downstream imputation should not treat it as ignorable by default.
bite_note: Versus leaving inf in or clipping to the largest finite value, NaN keeps a fabricated extreme value out of means, fits and scaling.

failing_part: "values all lie at or below 1 holds fractions rather than percentages"
narrowest_regime: A percent-of-energy column whose maximum is at or below 1 and which is not a genuinely small-percentage nutrient or a near-all-zero column (for example alcohol in a pediatric or abstaining sample, omega-3, trans fat) - there it is more likely fractions; the out-of-range rule (below 0 or above 100) is sound
reason: Values outside 0-100 cannot be percent of energy, so that refusal holds. But a column with max <= 1 can be genuine percentages: alcohol %kcal in children or abstainers is all 0, and minor items such as EPA+DHA %kcal are around 0.1-0.5. The rule is a heuristic stated as fact with no basis, and it would refuse valid data (or mis-scale a swap if it silently converted).
bite_note: Decides whether a share swap computes; a false positive blocks valid data, and a fraction column accepted as percent would change energy shares by 100x.

narrowest_regime: Standard drinks as defined by governments; self-defined 'drinks' or larger-than-standard servings should be converted to grams of ethanol directly
reason: Kalinowski & Humphreys 2016 report standard drinks of 8-20 g across 37 countries with a typical 10 g (verified in the abstract); US 14 g (NIAAA) and UK unit 8 g (10 mL ethanol) are correct, and 7 kcal/g is the Atwater factor for ethanol, so 7 x grams per drink is right. Rejecting sizes outside the documented governmental range is a sensible guard for a 'standard drink' column; it is a convention, not a theorem.

citations.cite: Kalinowski & Humphreys 2016 Addiction 111:1293 (abstract: typical 10 g, range 8-20 g)
NIAAA standard drink 14 g; NHS unit 8 g; Atwater 7 kcal/g ethanol (standard, not re-fetched)

bite_note: Drink size scales kcal per drink 2.5-fold (56 to 140 kcal), so the chosen size drives the substitution result.

narrowest_regime: Reliable only when k is not tiny; at k = 3 the t(1) multiplier is about 12.7 and tau-hat is very noisy, so the interval is a minimum-information statement; performance measures should be pooled on a suitable (e.g. logit/log) scale
reason: The interval mu-hat +/- t(k-2) sqrt(tau^2 + SE(mu)^2) is Higgins, Thompson & Spiegelhalter's approximate predictive interval for a new site, needing k >= 3 for df >= 1, and Riley et al. recommend reporting it for performance across validation settings. I-squared is a ratio of between to total variance, so it tends to 100% as site sizes grow even when absolute heterogeneity is small, which is why it can mislead for large sites.

citations.cite: Higgins, Thompson & Spiegelhalter 2009 JRSS A 172:137 (proposes the simple prediction interval; abstract fetched)
Riley et al. 2016 BMJ 353:i3140 (article exists; recommendation text not retrieved)
Rucker et al. 2008 BMC Med Res Methodol 8:79 (I-squared depends on study size)
Partlett & Riley 2017 Stat Med (PI coverage poor with small k)

bite_note: With large sites I-squared can read near 100% while the prediction interval is clinically narrow (or the reverse), so which summary leads changes whether a model is judged transportable.

failing_part: fitting conditional logistic regression and adding the log of the control sampling fraction to the model's intercept
narrowest_regime: Unconditional logistic regression on unmatched (or frequency-matched, with matching factors in the model) case-control data with known case and control sampling fractions; for individually matched or nested case-control sets use risk-set-based estimators (Langholz & Borgan 1997) that combine the matched-set relative-risk estimates with external or cohort incidence
reason: Conditional logistic regression conditions the stratum-specific intercepts away, so there is no intercept to shift and no baseline risk; it identifies only odds ratios (or hazard ratios). The Prentice-Pyke result is that unconditional logistic regression on retrospectively sampled data gives the right slopes and an intercept offset by log(pi1/pi0), which reduces to the control sampling fraction only if all cases are sampled. Applying it to conditional logit is a misapplication, and the matching factors' effects on risk are also lost.

citations.cite: Prentice & Pyke 1979 Biometrika 66:403 (unconditional logistic; intercept shift by sampling fractions)
Langholz & Borgan 1997 Biometrics 53:767 'Estimation of absolute risk from nested case-control data' (abstract: individually matched designs need extended methods beyond unmatched approaches)

bite_note: Computing absolute risks from a matched design by this recipe yields a number with no valid baseline; a researcher would otherwise use a nested-case-control absolute-risk method or an external incidence.

failing_part: "with at least 90% of refits succeeding this barely moves it"
narrowest_regime: Failures that are unrelated to the statistic (random failures), or informative failures at a rate small enough that the dropped share is well under the percentile tail mass (a few percent for a 95% band)
reason: Conditioning on fittable resamples is the right diagnosis, but 'barely moves' holds only when failures are non-informative. In the stated regime (resamples missing a class) failures are concentrated in one tail of the statistic: in my simulation (n=60, 10% prevalence, predicted risk), dropping 8.7% informative failures moved the 2.5th-percentile bound from 0.0055 to 0.0205, while random failures of 10-30% did not move it. The 90% cut-off is, as the basis says, a convention with no derivation.

citations.cite: Own simulation boot_fail.py (informative vs random failed refits)

bite_note: Decides whether the band is drawn; a band drawn at 90-97% success can still have a materially shifted tail, and a band refused at 85% may be fine if failures are random.

narrowest_regime: Eligibility defined on the analysis outcome; prespecified entry thresholds on a baseline-measured version of a variable are a different column and unaffected
reason: Choosing a cut after seeing the outcome distribution is a researcher degree of freedom, and truncating or selecting on the outcome attenuates associations, breaks causal contrasts and cannot be reproduced at deployment, so withholding the distribution and refusing outcome-based ranges is a consistent policy. The ban is broader than the 'data-driven' reason, but the underlying selection-on-the-outcome bias holds even for a prespecified cut, so the policy survives. It rests on an internal rule, not a cited source.

citations.cite: Heckman 1979 Econometrica 47:153 (selection bias, selection on the dependent variable) - from memory

bite_note: Removes the option to trim or select rows on outcome values at the eligibility step, which would otherwise change effect estimates and model performance.

failing_part: "always warrants a decision ... regardless of materiality"
narrowest_regime: Small n relative to p with an unpenalized linear or GLM learner, or when the deployment correlation structure may differ from training; for penalized or tree-based learners, or large n, the pair is immaterial for prediction
reason: Collinearity inflates coefficient variance and obscures attribution, but predictions under the same joint distribution are largely unaffected. In my simulation (two predictors, r = 0.95), a ridge fit changed out-of-sample MSE by 0.1% at n=500 and 1.2% at n=30, and r = 0.99 changed it by 0.1%. A fixed Decide for every |r| >= 0.9 pair ignores that the effect is often negligible.

citations.cite: Own simulation collin.py (OLS vs ridge vs drop-one, n = 30-500, r = 0.95-0.99)
Dormann et al. 2013 Ecography 36:27 (collinearity matters for inference, little for prediction under same structure) - from memory

bite_note: Changes whether a prompt surfaces as a required Decide or as an informational note; the unneeded forced decision costs the researcher a choice with nearly no effect on predictive performance.
